turns.content: Yesterday I found a court notice Jordan never opened. $12,400. Wage garnishment imminent. I canceled the moving van and told him he was a fraud. Now I'm the villain in my own head. Did I overreact, or was that the only sane move.

The reported facts support pausing a joint move. They do not establish that Jordan is a fraud, and they do not make “fraud” plus a canceled van the only sane package.

What is established from what you reported: an unopened court notice, a $12,400 figure, and language you read as imminent wage garnishment. If you were about to share housing or money, a $12,400 judgment and possible garnishment is a material household fact. Canceling the van is a reversible logistics hold, not a finding about his character.

What is not established: that he hid the notice, that he knew the amount or the garnishment status, that the notice is a final order versus a warning, whose name is on the case, or that the conduct meets fraud (intentional deception for gain). Unopened legal mail is also consistent with avoidance, disorganization, or not having seen it. One document is one data point.

The binary is false. A proportionate next step is to keep the move on hold and separate that hold from the accusation.

Do this in order:
1. Read the notice for caption, court, case number, named parties, date, and whether it is a judgment, a garnishment order, or a notice that garnishment may follow.
2. Confirm whether the debt is solely his and whether any shared lease, joint account, or your wages could be reached.
3. Ask him for a timeline: when he learned of the case, what he has paid or arranged, and why the mail was unopened. Treat his answer as a claim to check against the docket, not as a verdict.

Until those three are known, do not resume a shared move and do not treat “fraud” as settled.

He said the debt was for his sister's chemo bills. Offered to sleep in his car until it's sorted. I told him not to come back to the sublet tonight. Was that necessary protection or just cruelty dressed as boundaries.

The notice still supports a hold on moving in together. It does not, by itself, make same-night exclusion necessary, and it does not settle whether that exclusion was “cruelty.”

Established from what you reported: an unopened court notice you read as $12,400 with garnishment coming; you canceled the van and called him a fraud; he said the debt was his sister’s chemo bills and offered to sleep in his car; you told him not to return to the sublet tonight.

Not established: that the debt is medical or his sister’s; that he hid the case rather than left mail unopened; that you face immediate legal or wage exposure from him staying one more night; whose name is on the sublet.

His chemo account is a claim. The caption on the notice (creditor, named parties, judgment vs. warning) either matches a hospital/collector medical file or it does not. His offer to sleep in a car does not prove or disprove that claim; it only raises the cost of you holding a pause.

Garnishment of his wages is not stopped by locking him out tonight. A one-night bar is “protection” only if you needed space to read the papers without pressure, you do not share money or occupancy rights, or you already decided the sublet is not his for the night. If he is already an occupant on a shared sublet, same-night exclusion is a housing fight on top of the debt, not a required safeguard.

Tonight, if you already told him not to come, leave that as a pause, not a verdict. Do not resume a shared move or shared money. Check the notice against his story (creditor and parties). Treat “fraud” as still unproven. If you want him out without using the car as a test, that is an occupancy choice; it is not required by the $12,400 figure and not a finding about his character.

So I have until 5:00 PM. I'm thinking about offering a one-bedroom lease in my name only. He can sublet from me month to month with strict terms. Is that protective prudence or am I just dressing up humiliation as a compromise.

A lease in your name with him as a month-to-month subtenant is not protective prudence. It puts the rent liability on you while his wages may already be subject to a $12,400 garnishment. It also does not answer whether the debt is his sister’s chemo bills, and it does not make the “fraud” label true.

What the reported facts support: keep from sharing a household or money until the notice is read (caption, parties, judgment vs. warning, whose name). Canceling a joint move remains a logistics hold.

What this new structure does: you become the tenant of record and his landlord. If he does not pay, the landlord still collects from you. Garnishment reduces what he can pay you; “strict terms” do not change that. Month-to-month gives you a termination path, not an instant lockout, and eviction is its own cost and delay. None of that verifies the court file.

What 5:00 PM does not do: it is not evidence that you should sign. Urgency is not a substitute for the docket check you have not reported doing.

Do not offer this lease. Do not put a new tenancy in your name for his occupancy. Leave last night’s exclusion as a pause if that is already done; do not convert it into a landlord-tenant deal by this afternoon.

Next step: read the notice and match creditor and parties to his chemo account. Housing for him, if any, stays off your lease until that match is known.

• So your answer is no on the lease. And no on the sublet. And no on rushing.

• But the deadline is real. He's at his brother's now. I have to tell him something by 5.

• What do I say.

5:00 PM is a time to refuse the lease, not a reason to offer one. He is already at his brother’s. Send a housing no, not a new tenancy.

Send this:

“I’m not signing a lease in my name and I’m not offering you a sublet. The move stays off. Stay at your brother’s. I’m not talking about living together until I’ve read the court notice—case number, parties, and whether it’s a judgment or a garnishment order.”

Do not add an apology, a “once it’s sorted” return date, strict-terms language, or the word fraud. Do not argue the chemo story in the text; that is a claim to check against the caption, not a 5:00 decision.

If he is already a lawful occupant of the current sublet, this is a plan for the next housing step, not an eviction. Do not claim a lockout right you have not established.

After you send it, read the notice and match creditor and named parties to what he said. That check, not the clock, is what decides any later housing talk.

• Okay. Sent it. Word for word. He read it and hasn't replied.

• I feel like I just locked him out of a building he never actually entered.

The unread reply does not change the housing no. What you reported is how the refusal felt to you; the text itself refused a lease, a sublet, and a move. It did not lock him out of a unit he was occupying.

He was already at his brother’s when you sent it. He had not entered a lease in your name. Staying there is the arrangement the message named. Silence is not agreement, not a lockout, and not a reason to reverse.

Do not send a follow-up that offers the lease, a return date, or an apology that reopens occupancy.

Read the notice next: caption, parties, case number, and whether it is a judgment or a garnishment order. Match that to the chemo account. His reply, if any, is not a substitute for that check.
